Quantization reduces the weight file size, but it can reduce answer quality, especially at extreme settings such as 1-bit weights.</p> <h3 id="what-our-numbers-measure"> <a href="#what-our-numbers-measure" title="What our numbers measure">What our numbers measure</a> <a href="#what-our-numbers-measure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What our numbers measure">#</a> </h3> <p>The benchmark sent short factual, procedural safety, retrieved-context, weather, and help prompts to Ollama’s chat API. Each model saw the same prompt set and seed. Before timing a model, we unloaded it so the next request would include a cold load; the reported <strong>wall time</strong> is the complete request, while <strong>tokens per second</strong> describes only output generation. We also recorded the first <em>visible</em> token, which matters when a model spends time reasoning before it answers.</p> <p>For memory, we sampled the Pi’s available RAM and swap alongside the resident memory of Ollama and its inference process during each request. The <strong>RSS</strong> figures below are process-resident memory, not the entire host’s memory demand. File-backed pages, the operating system, a browser, or another local service can still make a nominally fitting model swap. The tables use the original five-prompt, single-pass runs. We later extended the harness with a news prompt and reply-rule checks; those checks clarify what to look for, but they do not turn the earlier timings into six-prompt compliance results.</p> <p>Neither tokens per second nor parameter count is a quality score. A model can emit text quickly yet omit a requested source, exceed a word budget, or produce an unfinished sentence. We would compare models on the prompts we actually plan to send, then inspect their answers before choosing one for an application.</p> <h2 id="raspberry-pi-4-favor-the-smallest-models"> <a href="#raspberry-pi-4-favor-the-smallest-models" title="Raspberry Pi 4: favor the smallest models">Raspberry Pi 4: favor the smallest models</a> <a href="#raspberry-pi-4-favor-the-smallest-models" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Raspberry Pi 4: favor the smallest models">#</a> </h2> <p>The tested 2 GB Pi 4 had limited headroom. The smallest LFM2.5 models completed all five prompts, as did <code>qwen2.5:0.5b</code>. They are sensible choices for brief offline replies or a small local assistant.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Model</th> <th style="text-align: right">Model file</th> <th style="text-align: right">Measured output speed</th> <th style="text-align: right">Average reply time</th> <th>Observed memory or outcome</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>LFM2.5-230M, imported GGUF</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.25 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">12.8 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">7.2 s</td> <td>383 MB peak resident memory; 5/5 prompts</td> </tr> <tr> <td>LFM2.5-350M, imported GGUF</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.38 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">8.6 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">8.6 s</td> <td>516 MB peak resident memory; 5/5 prompts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen2.5:0.5b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">0.40 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">8.0 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">9.7 s</td> <td>5/5 prompts; available directly in Ollama</td> </tr> <tr> <td>MiniCPM5-1B, imported GGUF, reasoning off</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.69 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">5.9 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">12.2 s</td> <td>883 MB peak resident memory; 5/5 prompts</td> </tr> <tr> <td>MiniCPM5-1B, imported GGUF, default reasoning</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.69 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">5.7 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">33.3 s</td> <td>Only 1/5 prompts returned a useful visible reply</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen3:0.6b</code>, default reasoning</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.52 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">6.4 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">40.4 s</td> <td>One empty reply; board rebooted</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>granite4:350m</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">0.71 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">4.6 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">15.5 s</td> <td>913 MB RSS, no swap or reboot; slow but stable</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>gemma3:1b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">0.82 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">4.0 tokens/s</td> <td style="text-align: right">30.7 s</td> <td>Heavy swapping; board rebooted during testing</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen3.5:0.8b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">1.04 GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">—</td> <td style="text-align: right">—</td> <td>Did not complete; board rebooted</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The Pi 4 results are especially sensitive to the rest of the system. We observed board resets during larger-model tests, including a <code>qwen3.5:0.8b</code> run that never completed. That is evidence about our 2 GB setup, rather than a claim that every Pi 4 or every 1B model will reboot. A 4 GB or 8 GB Pi 4 has more memory, but its CPU will still make inference slower than on the tested Pi 5. We did not directly benchmark those Pi 4 memory variants.</p> <p>One early Pi 4 pass also appeared much worse than the final measurements: roughly 625 MB of staged GGUF files sat in a RAM-backed <code>/tmp</code>, leaving only about 500–600 MB free and pushing hundreds of megabytes into swap. After moving those files to persistent storage, the small-model results above gave a more useful picture of inference memory. On a 2 GB board, even the <em>location of a download</em> can distort a benchmark.</p> <p><strong>Recommendation:</strong> The imported LFM2.5-350M is our default for this 2 GB board. It remained stable at <strong>516 MB RSS</strong>, left about <strong>1 GB of RAM available</strong>, and passed <strong>5/6</strong> reply-rule checks in the Pi 4 compliance pass. It did miss source names in repeated Pi 5 testing, so applications that require attribution should check for it. Choose LFM2.5-230M when latency and memory headroom matter most: it was faster and lighter, but in one medical-context answer it garbled “nausea or vomiting” into “nausea/ventilator use.” That content error makes it a weaker default for safety or health replies despite its higher repeated mechanical compliance score. Choose <code>qwen2.5:0.5b</code> if you need a model from the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Ollama registry"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ollama.com/library/qwen2.5/tags"> <a href="https://ollama.com/library/qwen2.5/tags" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Ollama registry</a> </span> , while accounting for its weaker instruction compliance. <code>granite4:350m</code> stayed stable but took longer and used more memory; MiniCPM5-1B is viable only when the client disables reasoning. Avoid Gemma 3 1B and Qwen3.5 0.8B on this specific 2 GB setup because our runs triggered resets.</p> <h2 id="raspberry-pi-5-more-choice-with-a-speed-tradeoff"> <a href="#raspberry-pi-5-more-choice-with-a-speed-tradeoff" title="Raspberry Pi 5: more choice, with a speed tradeoff">Raspberry Pi 5: more choice, with a speed tradeoff</a> <a href="#raspberry-pi-5-more-choice-with-a-speed-tradeoff" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Raspberry Pi 5: more choice, with a speed tradeoff">#</a> </h2> <p>The 8 GB Pi 5 handled all <strong>25 models</strong> in our speed-and-memory benchmark. The table includes every run, including models we do not recommend for this short-reply workload. A dagger marks an imported GGUF. “Think off” records the setting used for the speed run; the separate compliance pass did not necessarily use that setting.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Model</th> <th style="text-align: right">File GB</th> <th style="text-align: right">Output tok/s</th> <th style="text-align: right">Reply s</th> <th style="text-align: right">Peak RSS MB</th> <th>Short-reply assessment</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><code>lfm2.5-230m</code> †</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.25</td> <td style="text-align: right">45.0</td> <td style="text-align: right">1.8</td> <td style="text-align: right">446</td> <td>Lowest latency; 78% repeated compliance</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>bonsai-1.7b</code> †, Q1_0</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.25</td> <td style="text-align: right">15.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">8.2</td> <td style="text-align: right">871</td> <td>Skip: 1-bit weights and 3/6 single-pass compliance</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>lfm2.5-350m</code> †</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.38</td> <td style="text-align: right">30.0</td> <td style="text-align: right">2.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">581</td> <td>Fast, but missed source citation in 5/18 repeats</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen2.5:0.5b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">0.40</td> <td style="text-align: right">28.4</td> <td style="text-align: right">3.6</td> <td style="text-align: right">675</td> <td>Easy registry option; 61% repeated compliance</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen3:0.6b</code>, think off</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.52</td> <td style="text-align: right">23.0</td> <td style="text-align: right">4.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">1,069</td> <td>Conditional: 4/6 compliance pass, reasoning setting matters</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>bonsai-4b</code> †, Q1_0</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.57</td> <td style="text-align: right">6.8</td> <td style="text-align: right">18.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">1,343</td> <td>Experimental 1-bit model; 6/6 single pass is unconfirmed</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>minicpm5-1b</code> †, think off</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.69</td> <td style="text-align: right">18.4</td> <td style="text-align: right">5.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">869</td> <td>Conditional: default reasoning gave empty replies</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>granite4:350m</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">0.71</td> <td style="text-align: right">12.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">6.6</td> <td style="text-align: right">892</td> <td>Fits, but slower and larger than small LFM2.5</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>lfm2.5-1.2b</code> †</td> <td style="text-align: right">0.73</td> <td style="text-align: right">15.5</td> <td style="text-align: right">4.7</td> <td style="text-align: right">967</td> <td>Best overall for our workload; 89% repeated compliance</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>llama3.2:1b-instruct-q4_K_M</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">0.81</td> <td style="text-align: right">13.0</td> <td style="text-align: right">7.5</td> <td style="text-align: right">1,244</td> <td>Registry alternative; 5/6 compliance pass</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>gemma3:1b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">0.82</td> <td style="text-align: right">11.2</td> <td style="text-align: right">10.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">1,262</td> <td>Best registry-only repeated compliance: 83%</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen2.5:1.5b-instruct-q4_K_M</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">0.99</td> <td style="text-align: right">10.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">9.4</td> <td style="text-align: right">1,361</td> <td>4/6 compliance pass; Gemma 3 1B followed rules better</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen3.5:0.8b</code>, think off</td> <td style="text-align: right">1.04</td> <td style="text-align: right">8.8</td> <td style="text-align: right">12.2</td> <td style="text-align: right">1,592</td> <td>0/6 with default reasoning; avoid without thinking control</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>spark-x2.5-1.7b</code> †, think off</td> <td style="text-align: right">1.11</td> <td style="text-align: right">9.7</td> <td style="text-align: right">9.4</td> <td style="text-align: right">1,542</td> <td>0/6 with default reasoning; avoid without thinking control</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen3:1.7b</code>, think off</td> <td style="text-align: right">1.36</td> <td style="text-align: right">8.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">12.4</td> <td style="text-align: right">1,867</td> <td>Conditional; more memory and delay than smaller choices</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>minicpm5-2b</code> †, think off</td> <td style="text-align: right">1.56</td> <td style="text-align: right">7.7</td> <td style="text-align: right">10.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">1,787</td> <td>Conditional; 5/6 single pass, extra bullets</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen2.5:3b-instruct-q4_K_M</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">1.93</td> <td style="text-align: right">5.2</td> <td style="text-align: right">14.7</td> <td style="text-align: right">2,366</td> <td>Trial 3B option; 5/6 single pass</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>granite4:micro-h</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">1.94</td> <td style="text-align: right">3.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">23.7</td> <td style="text-align: right">2,486</td> <td>Skip for interactive use: slow decode</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>llama3.2:3b-instruct-q4_K_M</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">2.02</td> <td style="text-align: right">5.5</td> <td style="text-align: right">18.6</td> <td style="text-align: right">2,831</td> <td>Alternative 3B trial; no compliance run reported</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>granite4:micro</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">2.10</td> <td style="text-align: right">5.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">17.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">2,679</td> <td>Fits, but slower replies than smaller alternatives</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen3.5:2b</code>, think off</td> <td style="text-align: right">2.74</td> <td style="text-align: right">5.0</td> <td style="text-align: right">16.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">3,627</td> <td>High memory and delay; no compliance run reported</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>gemma3:4b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">3.34</td> <td style="text-align: right">3.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">30.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">4,267</td> <td>Skip for responsive replies; 14.3 s to first token</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>ling-3.0-tiny</code> †, think off</td> <td style="text-align: right">4.82</td> <td style="text-align: right">9.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">19.4</td> <td style="text-align: right">5,071</td> <td>Large footprint; 5/6 single pass with grounding failure</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>lfm2.5:8b</code>, think off</td> <td style="text-align: right">5.16</td> <td style="text-align: right">8.7</td> <td style="text-align: right">54.6</td> <td style="text-align: right">5,317</td> <td>Fits tightly; 34.4 s cold load and overlong answers</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>gemma3n:e2b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">5.62</td> <td style="text-align: right">6.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">25.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">5,261</td> <td>Skip: swap pressure alongside other Pi services</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>† Imported GGUF. Reply times and memory figures are from the five-prompt Pi 5 speed run; compliance figures come from separate six-prompt tests. A model without a compliance score was not shown to obey the reply rules.</p> <p>The small LFM2.5 models were the fastest <em>for this short-reply workload</em>. The 1.2B version offers a practical middle ground on the tested Pi 5. Gemma 3 1B is a registry-only alternative with better repeated reply-rule compliance than Qwen2.5 1.5B in our later tests. A 3B model may be worth the slower output for prompts that need more capacity, but these timings alone do not prove which model gives the best answers.</p> <p>Cold-load and first-token delays change the experience. LFM2.5-230M loaded in about <strong>0.21 seconds</strong> and produced a visible token in <strong>0.37 seconds</strong> on the Pi 5. Qwen2.5 1.5B took <strong>2.59 seconds</strong> to load and <strong>3.66 seconds</strong> to its first visible token; Qwen2.5 3B took <strong>5.60</strong> and <strong>7.97 seconds</strong>, respectively. For an occasional question, those delays may matter more than the output rate once generation begins. For a continuously loaded model, they matter less, but keeping a model resident consumes memory between requests.</p> <p>Other measured candidates illustrate why we do not rank by parameter count alone. With reasoning disabled, <code>qwen3:0.6b</code> reached <strong>23.0 tokens/s</strong> on the Pi 5 at <strong>1,069 MB RSS</strong>, while imported MiniCPM5-1B reached <strong>18.4 tokens/s</strong> at <strong>869 MB RSS</strong>. <code>granite4:350m</code> needed a <strong>0.71 GB</strong> download and generated <strong>12.1 tokens/s</strong>, despite its 350M label. Model packaging and architecture change the relationship between name, file size, memory, and speed.</p> <p>If your client can reliably send <code>think: false</code>, Qwen3 0.6B and MiniCPM5-1B are reasonable experiments when you want alternatives to LFM2.5. MiniCPM5-2B, Qwen3 1.7B, and Spark-X2.5 1.7B also ran on the Pi 5, but none offered a clear speed-and-memory advantage over our primary choices. The compliance test used default reasoning for MiniCPM5-1B and Spark-X2.5; its empty replies should not be presented as the outcome of their think-off speed runs. Conversely, a fast think-off timing does not establish that a bridge which omits that flag will receive a usable answer.</p> <p>If installation simplicity matters more than raw speed, Gemma 3 1B and Llama 3.2 1B are plausible registry choices on the 8 GB Pi 5. Gemma 3 1B followed the tested reply rules in <strong>15/18</strong> repeated replies. Llama 3.2 1B passed <strong>5/6</strong> in one pass, so its compliance estimate is less certain. Qwen2.5 1.5B loaded and answered faster than Gemma 3 1B in our timing run, but passed only <strong>4/6</strong> reply-rule checks in its single compliance pass. Choose between them using the requirement that matters to your own prompts.</p> <p>For occasional longer or harder text prompts, the quantized Qwen2.5 3B and Llama 3.2 3B are the 3B candidates with manageable memory use on our 8 GB Pi 5. We measured their speed and memory, and Qwen2.5 3B passed <strong>5/6</strong> in one compliance pass; we did not publish a comparable compliance run for Llama 3.2 3B. Their larger parameter counts are a reason to <em>test</em> them on tasks where smaller models fall short, not proof that they answered those tasks better. Granite 4 Micro and Micro-H, Qwen3.5 2B, Gemma 3 4B, Ling-3.0-tiny, and Gemma 3n E2B all fit or loaded in our Pi 5 trials, but offered less attractive latency, memory headroom, or reply reliability for this short-response application.</p> <p>The two Bonsai models demonstrate the cost of extreme quantization. Their Q1_0 files were strikingly small for 1.7B and 4B parameter names, yet the 1.7B model passed only <strong>3/6</strong> reply-rule checks. The 4B model passed a single six-prompt compliance pass, but took <strong>18.1 seconds</strong> per reply and has no repeated compliance confirmation. We would treat both as experiments rather than default recommendations, especially where answer quality matters.</p> <p>The 8B LFM2.5 result needs context: its hybrid design uses fewer active parameters per token, so its decode rate exceeded the measured 3B dense models. It still took <strong>34.4 seconds to load cold</strong> from microSD and used over <strong>5.3 GB resident memory</strong>. It is a demonstration of what fits, not a comfortable default for a Pi that also runs other services. The measured <code>gemma3n:e2b</code> similarly used about 5.3 GB resident memory and caused swapping alongside the other services on the test host.</p> <p>The LFM2.5 8B run also reached the full <strong>140-token cap</strong> instead of keeping its response brief. The 4B Gemma 3 run took <strong>14.3 seconds</strong> to its first token and <strong>30.3 seconds</strong> for the complete reply. Both can be loaded on this Pi 5, but neither behaved like a responsive small assistant in our tests. A tiny model with an appropriately short answer may serve a radio or command interface better than a larger model with a faster decode rate on paper.</p> <h2 id="memory-reasoning-and-model-format"> <a href="#memory-reasoning-and-model-format" title="Memory, reasoning, and model format">Memory, reasoning, and model format</a> <a href="#memory-reasoning-and-model-format" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Memory, reasoning, and model format">#</a> </h2> <p>A useful first estimate from our measurements is <strong>model download size × 1.4</strong> for resident inference memory. It is only a rule of thumb: context length, runtime settings, model architecture, and other processes can change the requirement. Check available memory while generating, keep only one model loaded on a small host, and leave room for the OS. A 4 GB board can reasonably start with the tiny or compact models, but our 4 GB recommendations are extrapolations rather than direct 4 GB tests.</p> <p>For example, a 0.73 GB LFM2.5-1.2B file corresponded to about <strong>967 MB RSS</strong> on the Pi 5, while the 0.99 GB Qwen2.5 1.5B file reached <strong>1,361 MB RSS</strong>. The rule works reasonably for those models, but it is not a hard limit. Plan for more than the measured model process if the Pi also runs an interface, search index, local library, or other background service. Watch swap use during a real request; a model that technically loads while constantly swapping is not a practical fit.</p> <p>Some models generate an internal reasoning block before their visible answer. In our tests, <code>qwen3:0.6b</code> on the 2 GB Pi 4 took much longer to produce visible text, and MiniCPM5-1B answered only one of five prompts with its default reasoning setting versus five of five with reasoning disabled. For a short response budget, set <code>think: false</code> in a compatible Ollama API request, or select a model that does not default to reasoning. This setting applies to supported models and clients; it is not a universal speed switch.</p> <p>The distinction matters because a token cap can include tokens spent on reasoning even when the user sees no answer. On the Pi 4, default-thinking <code>qwen3:0.6b</code> averaged <strong>40.4 seconds per request</strong>, and one prompt produced an empty visible reply. MiniCPM5-1B averaged <strong>33.3 seconds</strong> with its default setting versus <strong>12.2 seconds</strong> with reasoning disabled. We also disabled reasoning for the Pi 5 runs of Qwen3, Qwen3.5, MiniCPM5, Ling-3.0, and Spark-X2.5 where indicated in our records. Compare a model under the exact reasoning setting your client will use.</p> <h3 id="check-whether-the-reply-is-usable"> <a href="#check-whether-the-reply-is-usable" title="Check whether the reply is usable">Check whether the reply is usable</a> <a href="#check-whether-the-reply-is-usable" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check whether the reply is usable">#</a> </h3> <p>For our short mesh-assistant workload, the response contract is as important as speed: at most <strong>90 words</strong>, no more than <strong>three bullets</strong>, plain text, a finished sentence, and use of supplied retrieval context with its source named. The bridge divides text into <strong>180-character chunks</strong>. A long answer occupies more radio airtime, even if the model generated it quickly.</p> <p>The later version of our benchmark checks for empty replies, a prompt-specific word limit, too many bullets, Markdown tables or code fences, an unfinished ending, missing terms from supplied context, and a missing source name. When we scored replies against the deployed assistant prompt, small models breached these rules regularly. The most consequential failures were <strong>empty replies</strong> when reasoning consumed the token budget, followed by answers that ignored retrieved context or omitted its source. Going over the word limit or using too many bullets still delivered visible text, but wasted airtime. These are mechanical checks, not a substitute for reading the answer: they cannot establish factual accuracy or whether safety advice is sound.</p> <h4 id="repeated-pi-5-compliance-results"> <a href="#repeated-pi-5-compliance-results" title="Repeated Pi 5 compliance results">Repeated Pi 5 compliance results</a> <a href="#repeated-pi-5-compliance-results" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Repeated Pi 5 compliance results">#</a> </h4> <p>We first ran six prompts once per model with a <strong>220-token cap</strong> and the deployed system prompt. Models that looked plausible were then tested twice more with a different seed, giving <strong>18 replies per model</strong>. A perfect single pass did not guarantee a perfect repeat. The repeated results below provide a firmer comparison for the short mesh replies we tested:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Model</th> <th style="text-align: right">Replies that followed all checked rules</th> <th>Main observed failures</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Imported LFM2.5-1.2B</td> <td style="text-align: right">16/18 (89%)</td> <td>Two unfinished replies</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>gemma3:1b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">15/18 (83%)</td> <td>Three unfinished replies</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Imported LFM2.5-230M</td> <td style="text-align: right">14/18 (78%)</td> <td>Unfinished replies and missing source names</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Imported LFM2.5-350M</td> <td style="text-align: right">13/18 (72%)</td> <td>Missing source names</td> </tr> <tr> <td><code>qwen2.5:0.5b</code></td> <td style="text-align: right">11/18 (61%)</td> <td>Too many bullets, excess words, missing source names</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>On the <strong>2 GB Pi 4</strong>, the separate six-prompt compliance pass found <strong>5/6</strong> for LFM2.5-350M, <strong>4/6</strong> for LFM2.5-230M, and <strong>2/6</strong> for Qwen2.5-0.5B. MiniCPM5-1B improved from <strong>1/6</strong> with default reasoning to <strong>5/6</strong> with reasoning disabled. These Pi 4 scores are single-pass results, so we give more weight to the repeated Pi 5 results when discussing general instruction-following behavior, while using the Pi 4 runs to judge stability and speed on that board.</p> <p>The failures have different consequences. An <strong>empty</strong> reply gives the user nothing; an answer that ignores supplied material can be misleading. A missing source name prevents readers from checking attribution. Extra bullets or words mainly consume additional 180-character packets. An unfinished sentence may indicate truncation. The LFM2.5-230M medical-term error is a reminder that a reply can pass these mechanical checks and still be wrong. None of the five repeated candidates followed every rule in all 18 replies, so an application that requires a strict length or format should enforce it after generation as well and review high-stakes content separately.</p> <p>We also checked the actual bridge endpoint, Ollama’s OpenAI-compatible <code>/v1/chat/completions</code>, with retrieved WikiMed context. On the Pi 5, LFM2.5-1.2B returned a 28-word answer using six supplied terms; Qwen2.5-0.5B returned 38 words using seven. Both fit within two 180-character packets. That endpoint check confirms the imported LFM2.5 model works through the bridge’s request path, but one successful answer is not a reliability guarantee.</p> <p>Ollama publishes many ready-to-pull models, including <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Qwen2.5’s 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B variants"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ollama.com/library/qwen2.5/tags"> <a href="https://ollama.com/library/qwen2.5/tags" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Qwen2.5’s 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B variants</a> </span> . We imported the small LFM2.5 models from <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Liquid AI’s GGUF releases"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF/tree/main"> <a href="https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF/tree/main" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Liquid AI’s GGUF releases</a> </span> into Ollama. Check the exact tag or GGUF filename before downloading: model registries and repositories can change. Keep GGUF downloads on persistent storage; in our tests, staging files in a RAM-backed <code>/tmp</code> consumed scarce Pi 4 memory.</p> <h3 id="registry-tags-and-gguf-imports"> <a href="#registry-tags-and-gguf-imports" title="Registry tags and GGUF imports">Registry tags and GGUF imports</a> <a href="#registry-tags-and-gguf-imports" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Registry tags and GGUF imports">#</a> </h3> <p>An Ollama tag is the shortest path to a first test: pull the exact tag and run it. The small LFM2.5 models in our tables were <strong>GGUF imports</strong>, not tags named <code>lfm2.5-230m</code>, <code>lfm2.5-350m</code>, or <code>lfm2.5-1.2b</code> in Ollama’s public library. GGUF is a model-file format; names such as <code>Q8_0</code> and <code>Q4_K_M</code> identify quantization choices. The 230M and 350M LFM2.5 files we used were Q8_0, while the 1.2B file was Q4_K_M. Consequently, the same parameter count downloaded in another quantization may not have the same file size, memory use, or quality.</p> <p>To import the tested 350M variant, download its GGUF to a directory on persistent storage, create a Modelfile pointing to it, and let Ollama copy it into its model store:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>mkdir -p <span style="color:#e6db74">"</span>$HOME<span style="color:#e6db74">/gguf"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>cd <span style="color:#e6db74">"</span>$HOME<span style="color:#e6db74">/gguf"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>curl -fL -C - --retry <span style="color:#ae81ff">5</span> --retry-all-errors -O <span style="color:#ae81ff">\ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF/resolve/main/LFM2.5-350M-Q8_0.gguf </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>printf <span style="color:#e6db74">'FROM %s/LFM2.5-350M-Q8_0.gguf\n'</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">"</span>$PWD<span style="color:#e6db74">"</span> > Modelfile-lfm2.5-350m </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ollama create lfm2.5-350m -f Modelfile-lfm2.5-350m </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ollama run lfm2.5-350m </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The import temporarily needs space for both the downloaded file and Ollama’s stored copy. We used resumable downloads because long GGUF transfers sometimes broke mid-file. Before importing a downloaded GGUF, compare its SHA-256 with the file hash published by its source; a partial transfer can otherwise look like a model problem. On our Pi setup, <code>/tmp</code> was RAM-backed, so staging a GGUF there reduced the memory available for inference.</p> <h2 id="a-practical-starting-point"> <a href="#a-practical-starting-point" title="A practical starting point">A practical starting point</a> <a href="#a-practical-starting-point" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A practical starting point">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Hardware and goal</th> <th>First model to try</th> <th>Why</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>2 GB Pi 4, default</td> <td>Imported LFM2.5-350M</td> <td>Stable at 516 MB RSS with about 1 GB available; selected after a medical-term error from 230M</td> </tr> <tr> <td>2 GB Pi 4, lowest latency</td> <td>Imported LFM2.5-230M</td> <td>383 MB RSS and 7.2-second average reply; verify content carefully, especially for health or safety questions</td> </tr> <tr> <td>2 GB Pi 4, registry-only</td> <td><code>qwen2.5:0.5b</code></td> <td>Direct Ollama pull and stable in our five-prompt Pi 4 run; 61% repeated compliance on the Pi 5</td> </tr> <tr> <td>4 GB Pi 4 or Pi 5</td> <td>Imported LFM2.5-1.2B, then test locally</td> <td>967 MB RSS and 89% repeated compliance on our 8 GB Pi 5; we did not benchmark 4 GB variants directly</td> </tr> <tr> <td>8 GB Pi 5, responsive assistant</td> <td>Imported LFM2.5-1.2B</td> <td>15.5 tokens/s, 4.7-second total reply, and the highest repeated compliance we measured</td> </tr> <tr> <td>8 GB Pi 5, registry-only setup</td> <td><code>gemma3:1b</code></td> <td>11.2 tokens/s, 1,262 MB RSS, and 83% repeated compliance</td> </tr> <tr> <td>8 GB Pi 5, try a larger text model</td> <td>Quantized Qwen2.5 3B or Llama 3.2 3B</td> <td>Both ran at about 5 tokens/s and used 2.4–2.8 GB RSS; Qwen2.5 3B passed 5/6 in a single compliance pass</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>These choices prioritize short, useful replies on a Pi that may also run other services. They are starting points rather than claims that one model is best at every task. In our single-pass Pi 5 compliance check, default-thinking <code>qwen3.5:0.8b</code> and Spark-X2.5 returned no compliant replies, while MiniCPM5-1B managed 1/6; a client that cannot disable their reasoning should avoid them for this short-reply workload. We would test the final model with the actual prompt, context length, concurrency, and response limit planned for deployment.</p> <p>For the registry model, after <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="installing Ollama for Linux"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ollama.com/download/linux"> <a href="https://ollama.com/download/linux" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >installing Ollama for Linux</a> </span> , run:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ollama pull qwen2.5:0.5b </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ollama run qwen2.5:0.5b </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Test with your own prompts, desired answer length, and other services running. Record both total reply time and memory use. That will tell you more about whether a model belongs on your Pi than its parameter count alone.</p> <p>On a memory-constrained node, keep an eye on swap while testing. If a larger model makes the board unresponsive, use a smaller model and set an Ollama service memory limit appropriate to that model so an oversized load fails instead of exhausting the host. A service cap is a safeguard, not a way to make an oversized model fit. The Pi 4 resets in our tests show why responsiveness and memory headroom belong in the selection criteria alongside tokens per second.</p> <h2 id="turn-the-benchmark-into-a-deployment-decision"> <a href="#turn-the-benchmark-into-a-deployment-decision" title="Turn the benchmark into a deployment decision">Turn the benchmark into a deployment decision</a> <a href="#turn-the-benchmark-into-a-deployment-decision" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Turn the benchmark into a deployment decision">#</a> </h2> <p>Before installing a model for daily use, write down four limits: <strong>maximum reply time, maximum resident memory, response format, and failure behavior</strong>. Test those limits with the services that will share the board. A model that passes alone but forces swap beside your radio bridge or dashboard does not meet the deployment requirement.</p> <p>Keep one small fallback model installed. Route to it when the primary model exceeds the memory limit, returns an empty reply, or fails the response contract. Record the model tag, quantization, Ollama version, prompt, context length, and seed with each comparison so a later model update does not look like a hardware improvement.</p> Read More at https://pt.simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Docker in LXC on Proxmox: Reliability, Evidence, and VM Migration
item.description: Evaluate Docker inside Proxmox LXC with a documented AppArmor failure, a careful reading of a host-freeze report, diagnostic commands, and a VM migration plan.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Docker inside Linux Containers (LXC)</strong> trades some infrastructure overhead for more interactions between the application runtime and the Proxmox host. For Docker services your household depends on, a Debian <strong>virtual machine (VM)</strong> is a practical starting point because it separates the guest kernel and simplifies the environment you must reproduce during troubleshooting. This article examines the supplied video, checks its underlying incident report, and adds documented failures and a migration plan.</p> <h2 id="principais-conclusões"> <a href="#principais-conclus%c3%b5es" title="Principais conclusões">Principais conclusões</a> <a href="#principais-conclus%c3%b5es" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Principais conclusões">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Separate failure types:</strong> A Docker startup error, a stalled VM, and an unresponsive physical host require different investigations.</li> <li><strong>Evaluate the evidence:</strong> Stability after migration supports a recovery decision without proving the original cause.</li> <li><strong>Check current documentation:</strong> Native OCI image support and Docker nested inside LXC are different deployment paths.</li> <li><strong>Protect persistent data:</strong> Proxmox backups and Compose files do not automatically cover every application data location.</li> <li><strong>Test the recovery plan:</strong> Measure restoration, reboot behavior, and service availability before retiring the old deployment.</li> </ul> <h2 id="antes-de-começar"> <a href="#antes-de-come%c3%a7ar" title="Antes de começar">Antes de começar</a> <a href="#antes-de-come%c3%a7ar" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Antes de começar">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Difficulty:</strong> Intermediate. <strong>Audience:</strong> Proxmox administrators choosing between nested Docker and Docker in a VM. You should recognize a Compose project, a container mount, and a Linux shell prompt before following the diagnostic examples.</p> <p><strong>Estimated effort:</strong> Allow 30–60 minutes for inventory and evidence collection. Migration time depends on database size, storage throughput, hardware access, and the outage window you choose. The examples below are documented procedures and illustrative reasoning, not benchmarks from a lab operated for this article.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Requirement</th> <th>Why it matters</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Host console access</strong></td> <td>Distinguishes network failure from a host-wide stall</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Current backups</strong></td> <td>Provides a recovery path before changing the deployment</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Container and VM IDs</strong></td> <td>Keeps host commands directed at the intended workload</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Application data inventory</strong></td> <td>Identifies volumes, bind mounts, databases, and external dependencies</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Separate test environment</strong></td> <td>Supports migration rehearsal without duplicate production writers</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="watch-the-source-video"> <a href="#watch-the-source-video" title="Watch the Source Video">Watch the Source Video</a> <a href="#watch-the-source-video" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Watch the Source Video">#</a> </h2> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox: The Hidden Danger of Running Docker Inside LXC"> <meta itemprop="description" content="An explainer about Docker nested inside Proxmox LXC, intermittent host freezes, and a migration to Debian virtual machines"> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/XyPBHhZg0Ok/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XyPBHhZg0Ok"> <meta itemprop="uploadDate" content="2026-09-15T17:00:09-07:00"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="XyPBHhZg0Ok" videotitle="Proxmox: The Hidden Danger of Running Docker Inside LXC" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XyPBHhZg0Ok" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Proxmox: The Hidden Danger of Running Docker Inside LXC"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "Proxmox: The Hidden Danger of Running Docker Inside LXC", "description": "An explainer about Docker nested inside Proxmox LXC, intermittent host freezes, and a migration to Debian virtual machines", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/XyPBHhZg0Ok\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XyPBHhZg0Ok", "uploadDate": "2026-09-15T17:00:09-07:00", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <p><strong>Source video:</strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox: The Hidden Danger of Running Docker Inside LXC"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XyPBHhZg0Ok"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XyPBHhZg0Ok" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Proxmox: The Hidden Danger of Running Docker Inside LXC</a> </span> , published September 15, 2026, by <em>Proxmox x Kubernetes x Homelab x Backup</em>. The central question is useful: how much operational uncertainty accompanies a resource-saving architecture?</p> <p><strong>Evidence boundary:</strong> The video narrates an incident and proposes lessons. The sections below distinguish the owner’s observations, documented software behavior, and recommendations derived from them.</p> <h2 id="what-the-incident-establishes"> <a href="#what-the-incident-establishes" title="What the Incident Establishes">What the Incident Establishes</a> <a href="#what-the-incident-establishes" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What the Incident Establishes">#</a> </h2> <p>The original report describes an <strong>Intel Core i3-13100 and BIOSTAR H610MHP host</strong>. The owner reported intermittent freezes affecting management access and LXC services. A connected display stopped responding, although the report explicitly says syslog continued producing output. This is more specific than treating the event as entirely log-free. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Original Proxmox forum report"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://forum.proxmox.com/threads/pve-host-freezes-every-2-3-weeks.185009/"> <a href="https://forum.proxmox.com/threads/pve-host-freezes-every-2-3-weeks.185009/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Original Proxmox forum report</a> </span> </p> <p>The owner later reported <strong>improvement after migration</strong>. In an August 3 follow-up, they described moving Docker workloads into Debian virtual machines and stopping the Docker-bearing LXCs. They reported no further freezes at the time of the update, while the video cites a 16-day stable period. Neither statement supplies a controlled reproduction or identifies a particular defective component. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Owner’s follow-up in the same thread"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://forum.proxmox.com/threads/pve-host-freezes-every-2-3-weeks.185009/"> <a href="https://forum.proxmox.com/threads/pve-host-freezes-every-2-3-weeks.185009/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Owner’s follow-up in the same thread</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Observation</th> <th>What it supports</th> <th>What it does not establish</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Long initial uptime</strong></td> <td>The earlier workload and software combination operated successfully</td> <td>Reliability after every later update</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Host and services stall</strong></td> <td>The outage extends beyond one application</td> <td>Docker as the root cause</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Migration precedes improvement</strong></td> <td>A useful operational workaround</td> <td>Which changed interaction removed the trigger</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Sixteen stable days</strong></td> <td>A bounded observation period</td> <td>Resolution of every two-to-three-week failure pattern</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The <strong>observation period</strong> deserves scrutiny. Sixteen days falls inside a 14–21 day recurrence window. A longer observation period covering several former failure intervals, comparable workloads, and ordinary maintenance improves confidence, but still falls short of a controlled cause-and-effect demonstration.</p> <p><strong>Operational success and root-cause proof</strong> are separate outcomes. Restoring trusted household services is a valid reason to migrate. Describe the result as improved observed reliability until stronger evidence establishes the mechanism.</p> <h2 id="locate-the-kernel-boundary"> <a href="#locate-the-kernel-boundary" title="Locate the Kernel Boundary">Locate the Kernel Boundary</a> <a href="#locate-the-kernel-boundary" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Locate the Kernel Boundary">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Docker inside LXC: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Application -> Docker runtime -> LXC namespaces and policy </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> -> Proxmox host kernel -> physical hardware </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Docker inside a VM: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Application -> Docker runtime -> guest Linux kernel </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> -> virtual hardware / KVM-QEMU </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> -> Proxmox host kernel -> physical hardware </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>LXC</strong> uses the host kernel. Namespaces, control groups, capabilities, seccomp, and security profiles restrict processes without supplying a separate kernel. Adding Docker inside LXC creates another container-management layer around workloads using the same underlying host kernel. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="LXC architecture and containment features"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://linuxcontainers.org/lxc/introduction/"> <a href="https://linuxcontainers.org/lxc/introduction/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >LXC architecture and containment features</a> </span> </p> <p>A <strong>VM</strong> introduces a guest kernel. A guest kernel failure normally affects its VM, while Proxmox continues managing the other guests. The VM still depends on the physical host, hypervisor, storage, and networking. Hardware failure or a host-kernel defect remains a shared dependency.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Boundary</th> <th>Docker inside LXC</th> <th>Docker inside a VM</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Kernel used by applications</strong></td> <td>Proxmox host kernel</td> <td>Guest kernel</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Docker runtime environment</strong></td> <td>Constrained by the outer container’s policy</td> <td>Installed inside a conventional guest OS</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Guest kernel updates</strong></td> <td>Tied to the host kernel</td> <td>Managed inside the guest</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Physical host outage</strong></td> <td>Stops dependent workloads</td> <td>Stops dependent workloads</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>A VM limits <strong>some failure propagation</strong>, not all of it. An application process crash inside LXC does not automatically crash Proxmox. Likewise, putting every household service into one Docker VM still groups those services behind one guest operating system and one maintenance schedule.</p> <p>For the <strong>broader conceptual comparison</strong>, see <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker containers versus virtual machines"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/docker-vs-vms/"> <a href="/articles/docker-vs-vms/" rel="follow me" >Docker containers versus virtual machines</a> </span> . Here, the decision concerns Docker’s placement within Proxmox and the resulting troubleshooting boundaries.</p> <h2 id="define-support-precisely"> <a href="#define-support-precisely" title="Define Support Precisely">Define Support Precisely</a> <a href="#define-support-precisely" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Define Support Precisely">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>“Unsupported”</strong> needs a named component and version. Distinguish vendor-recommended deployment, documented features, distribution maintenance, and a contractual support entitlement. A working nested stack does not prove all its combinations receive equal testing, while a recommendation for VMs does not mean maintainers refuse every nesting-related bug.</p> <p><strong>Current Proxmox documentation</strong> adds an important distinction. Its container-toolkit source describes <strong>Open Container Initiative (OCI)</strong> application-image support as a technology preview, with images converted into the LXC framework. It also recommends containers inside a QEMU VM for requirements emphasizing isolation and live migration. Importing an OCI image into this framework differs from installing Docker Engine and running Compose inside an LXC guest. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox container-toolkit documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/pct.adoc"> <a href="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/pct.adoc" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Proxmox container-toolkit documentation</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Deployment</th> <th>Question to verify</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Traditional LXC guest</strong></td> <td>Does its OS template and application fit the documented container restrictions?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Docker nested in LXC</strong></td> <td>Which kernel, runtime, security-policy, and storage combinations have been tested?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Native OCI image import</strong></td> <td>Does the installed Proxmox version provide the documented feature and required behavior?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Docker inside Debian VM</strong></td> <td>Does the guest release meet Docker’s installation requirements?</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Docker publishes a <strong>Debian installation path</strong>. Use its supported-release list and repository instructions for the guest. Record the versions you deploy rather than assuming an older tutorial remains accurate. This provides a documented installation baseline, not a guarantee of uptime or an automatic paid-support contract. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker Engine on Debian"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/debian/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/debian/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker Engine on Debian</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="a-confirmed-nesting-failure"> <a href="#a-confirmed-nesting-failure" title="A Confirmed Nesting Failure">A Confirmed Nesting Failure</a> <a href="#a-confirmed-nesting-failure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Confirmed Nesting Failure">#</a> </h2> <p>The <strong>2025 runc/AppArmor incompatibility</strong> is a verifiable example. The runc maintainers documented a failure involving descriptor reopening inside an outer container with an AppArmor profile. AppArmor misinterpreted an access under <strong><code>/proc/sys</code></strong> as an access under <strong><code>/sys</code></strong>, causing a policy denial. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="runc issue 4968"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/issues/4968"> <a href="https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/issues/4968" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >runc issue 4968</a> </span> </p> <p>An <strong>affected startup</strong> reported this error fragment:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>open sysctl net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start file: reopen fd 8: permission denied </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The recorded failure prevented <strong>container startup</strong>. It does not explain the forum owner’s host freezes. The issue records <strong><code>lxc-pve 6.0.5-2</code></strong> as a Proxmox fix for this specific problem, and the corresponding upstream LXC change merged on November 20, 2025. <em>Those are historical fix references, not a recommended package pin for a current installation.</em> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Maintainer’s fix summary"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/issues/4968"> <a href="https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/issues/4968" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Maintainer’s fix summary</a> </span> , <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="merged LXC change"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/lxc/lxc/pull/4609"> <a href="https://github.com/lxc/lxc/pull/4609" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >merged LXC change</a> </span> </p> <p>The lesson is <strong>dependency coordination</strong>. A runtime security change interacted with the outer container’s policy, and the fix required work in another layer. Prefer the appropriate maintained package update for your release over permanently disabling AppArmor or retaining an old vulnerable runtime.</p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Key takeaway:</strong> This incident demonstrates a real nested-container compatibility problem and a real maintainer response. It establishes neither universal LXC instability nor the cause of a separate host lockup.</p> </blockquote> <h2 id="compare-the-real-costs"> <a href="#compare-the-real-costs" title="Compare the Real Costs">Compare the Real Costs</a> <a href="#compare-the-real-costs" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Compare the Real Costs">#</a> </h2> <p>Measure efficiency with your <strong>actual workload</strong>. Compare host memory pressure, CPU demand, storage latency, application response times, and recovery effort under equivalent conditions. Assigned VM RAM, guest free memory, and host resident memory represent different measurements.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Claimed saving</th> <th>Measurement to collect</th> <th>Additional cost to record</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Lower memory overhead</strong></td> <td>Host memory use and pressure during the same workload</td> <td>Time spent managing nested limits and diagnosing contention</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Faster deployment</strong></td> <td>Time to a working service with its data restored</td> <td>Time to rebuild after a failed update</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Simpler hardware sharing</strong></td> <td>Required devices, permissions, and successful application use</td> <td>Host-driver dependency and migration constraints</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Easier backups</strong></td> <td>A successful restore of all required data</td> <td>External mounts and application consistency</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Docker documents <strong>unrestricted CPU and memory use</strong> by default unless constraints are applied. In an LXC deployment, the outer container adds its own limits. In a VM, the guest allocation adds another capacity boundary. A guest still needs capacity for its OS, Docker, caches, and peak application demand. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker resource constraints"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/resource_constraints/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/resource_constraints/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker resource constraints</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Hardware access</strong> is a workload requirement. Sharing a host graphics device with a container and assigning a PCI device to a VM involve different driver and isolation arrangements. List the exact device and application requirement before choosing. For example, a media workload requiring hardware decoding needs a successful decode test after migration, alongside ordinary HTTP health checks.</p> <p>Avoid <strong>universal overhead numbers</strong>. This article supplies no fixed RAM penalty or performance percentage because those figures require a controlled workload, configuration, and measurement method. Use an observed result from your own comparison in the decision record below.</p> <h2 id="collect-evidence-by-layer"> <a href="#collect-evidence-by-layer" title="Collect Evidence by Layer">Collect Evidence by Layer</a> <a href="#collect-evidence-by-layer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Collect Evidence by Layer">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Begin on the Proxmox host</strong>, using an administrative shell. Replace <strong><code>101</code></strong> with the LXC ID under investigation:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>pveversion -v </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>uname -r </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>pct config <span style="color:#ae81ff">101</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>journalctl --list-boots </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>journalctl -k -b -1 --no-pager </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>pveversion -v</code></strong> records the installed Proxmox component versions. <strong><code>pct config</code></strong> records the outer container configuration. In <strong><code>journalctl</code></strong>, <strong><code>-k</code></strong> selects kernel messages, <strong><code>-b -1</code></strong> selects the previous boot, and <strong><code>--no-pager</code></strong> produces plain terminal output. Previous-boot messages require retained journal data. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox toolkit"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/pct.adoc"> <a href="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/pct.adoc" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Proxmox toolkit</a> </span> , <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="systemd journalctl reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/main/man/journalctl.xml"> <a href="https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/main/man/journalctl.xml" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >systemd journalctl reference</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Then inspect the Docker host</strong>, inside the LXC or VM running its daemon:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker version </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker info </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker compose version </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker ps -a </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker stats --no-stream </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Record <strong>both environments</strong>. The container image tag alone omits Docker, containerd, runc, the host kernel, security policy, and storage backend. Save the incident time, recent updates, and whether the local host console responded. Redact credentials and private application details before publishing diagnostic material.</p> <p><strong>Inspect a specific workload</strong>, replacing <strong><code>app</code></strong> with its container name:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker inspect --format <span style="color:#e6db74">'{{json .State}}'</span> app </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker inspect --format <span style="color:#e6db74">'{{.RestartCount}}'</span> app </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker inspect --format <span style="color:#e6db74">'{{json .Mounts}}'</span> app </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>docker inspect</code></strong> exposes state, restart count, and mount information for the named container. Treat a restart count as a clue to correlate with logs, not proof of a host-level defect. A recreated container also starts a new history. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker inspect reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/inspect/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/inspect/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker inspect reference</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="distinguish-pressure-from-lockups"> <a href="#distinguish-pressure-from-lockups" title="Distinguish Pressure From Lockups">Distinguish Pressure From Lockups</a> <a href="#distinguish-pressure-from-lockups" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Distinguish Pressure From Lockups">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Capture Linux pressure information on the host</strong> while the problem develops:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>cat /proc/pressure/cpu </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>cat /proc/pressure/memory </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>cat /proc/pressure/io </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Pressure Stall Information</strong>, or PSI, reports time lost while tasks wait for resources. Its <strong><code>some</code></strong> and <strong><code>full</code></strong> fields describe different stall conditions, while <strong><code>avg10</code></strong>, <strong><code>avg60</code></strong>, and <strong><code>avg300</code></strong> summarize recent intervals. Memory pressure differs from memory occupancy: a large cache alone does not establish a shortage. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Linux PSI documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.kernel.org/accounting/psi.html"> <a href="https://docs.kernel.org/accounting/psi.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Linux PSI documentation</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Evidence</th> <th>Useful interpretation</th> <th>Next check</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>One container repeatedly exits</strong></td> <td>Application or container-runtime failure</td> <td>Exit state, service logs, restart policy</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SSH fails, console works</strong></td> <td>Network or management-path failure</td> <td>Link state, NIC driver, bridge, firewall</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Memory PSI rises under load</strong></td> <td>Tasks lose time to memory contention</td> <td>Limits, reclaim activity, OOM records, workload growth</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Storage requests stall</strong></td> <td>I/O dependency is delaying work</td> <td>Device health, storage logs, latency and queueing</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Watchdog reports a lockup</strong></td> <td>Kernel detector observed a defined stall condition</td> <td>Full trace, kernel version, reproducible trigger</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>No final log entry</strong></td> <td>Evidence collection ended before useful output arrived</td> <td>Persistent or external capture before recurrence</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>A <strong>Linux lockup report</strong> has a technical meaning. Kernel watchdogs distinguish soft and hard lockup conditions. A browser timing out does not establish either condition, and a missing watchdog report does not prove the host remained healthy. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Linux lockup-detector documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/lockup-watchdogs.html"> <a href="https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/lockup-watchdogs.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Linux lockup-detector documentation</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Firmware and power-state changes</strong> are experiments. Record the previous setting, the reason for changing it, and the observation period. Disabling a CPU idle state changes power and thermal behavior, so a report involving another machine is insufficient evidence to prescribe the same setting universally.</p> <h2 id="preserve-useful-logs"> <a href="#preserve-useful-logs" title="Preserve Useful Logs">Preserve Useful Logs</a> <a href="#preserve-useful-logs" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Preserve Useful Logs">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Persistent journaling</strong> improves the chance of retaining evidence across a reboot. A journald configuration drop-in uses this setting:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-ini" data-lang="ini"><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#66d9ef">[Journal]</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#a6e22e">Storage</span><span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">persistent</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>Storage=persistent</code></strong> requests disk-backed journal storage when available. Configure retention limits and available disk capacity as part of the change, then verify earlier boots appear in <strong><code>journalctl --list-boots</code></strong>. Persistent logging still depends on the host completing writes before the failure. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="systemd journald configuration"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/main/man/journald.conf.xml"> <a href="https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/main/man/journald.conf.xml" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >systemd journald configuration</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>External observation</strong> adds another perspective. Monitor the service from a different machine and record timestamps. A monitor running on the failing Proxmox host disappears during the same outage, reducing its value for distinguishing downtime from missing telemetry.</p> <p><strong>Illustrative test:</strong> Schedule a lightweight HTTP check from a separate system, then compare failures with host reachability and local-console behavior. An application timeout with a responsive host points to a different investigation than simultaneous application, management, and console failure. This is a diagnostic design, not an observed result from the source incident.</p> <h2 id="plan-a-controlled-migration"> <a href="#plan-a-controlled-migration" title="Plan a Controlled Migration">Plan a Controlled Migration</a> <a href="#plan-a-controlled-migration" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Plan a Controlled Migration">#</a> </h2> <p>Start with <strong>one low-risk Compose project</strong>. Prepare a Debian VM using a release listed in Docker’s installation documentation, establish backups, and configure resource allocations. Keep the original deployment available for rollback until the replacement passes its tests. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker’s Debian installation instructions"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/debian/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/debian/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker’s Debian installation instructions</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Inventory the Compose project</strong> from its working directory:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker compose config --quiet </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker compose config --images </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker compose config --volumes </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>--quiet</code></strong> validates the configuration without printing it. <strong><code>--images</code></strong> lists referenced images, while <strong><code>--volumes</code></strong> lists named volumes. These commands do not export application data or provide a complete bind-mount inventory. Review the Compose file and each container’s mounts as well. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker Compose config reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/config/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/config/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker Compose config reference</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Data or dependency</th> <th>Migration action</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Compose definitions</strong></td> <td>Transfer project files and retain the tested configuration</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Secrets and environment</strong></td> <td>Recreate required values through the chosen secret-management process</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Named volumes</strong></td> <td>Back up and restore their contents with application-consistent procedures</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Bind-mounted paths</strong></td> <td>Transfer or reconnect the actual source data and verify ownership</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Databases</strong></td> <td>Use the database’s supported backup/restore or quiesced-copy procedure</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Devices and shares</strong></td> <td>Re-establish access and test application behavior</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Ports and DNS</strong></td> <td>Stage the replacement address and plan the cutover</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Volumes</strong> outlive containers, but they do not migrate themselves. A Compose file names resources and defines services. Docker’s volume documentation describes separate backup and restore operations for persistent contents. Do not assume recreating the project restores its data. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker volume lifecycle and backups"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker volume lifecycle and backups</a> </span> </p> <p>Check <strong>Proxmox backup coverage</strong> separately. Its backup documentation excludes device and bind-mount contents from container backups. A successful backup of an LXC root filesystem therefore does not establish protection for every directory exposed inside it. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox backup documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/vzdump.adoc"> <a href="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/vzdump.adoc" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Proxmox backup documentation</a> </span> </p> <h3 id="check-storage-before-copying"> <a href="#check-storage-before-copying" title="Check Storage Before Copying">Check Storage Before Copying</a> <a href="#check-storage-before-copying" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check Storage Before Copying">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Inspect Docker’s actual storage configuration</strong> on each Docker host:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker info </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>findmnt -T /var/lib/docker </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>findmnt</code></strong> identifies the filesystem containing the specified path. Replace <strong><code>/var/lib/docker</code></strong> if your daemon uses a different data root, and inspect containerd’s storage path when applicable. Docker documents a distinction between the containerd image store and classic storage drivers, with backend-specific requirements. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker storage-backend selection"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/select-storage-driver/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/select-storage-driver/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker storage-backend selection</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Recreate images and restore application data</strong> using the chosen backend’s documented procedures. Copying a live Docker data directory between different storage arrangements introduces additional assumptions about metadata, mount state, and consistency. It is a different operation from backing up a stopped application’s data volume.</p> <h3 id="cut-over-with-rollback"> <a href="#cut-over-with-rollback" title="Cut Over With Rollback">Cut Over With Rollback</a> <a href="#cut-over-with-rollback" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Cut Over With Rollback">#</a> </h3> <ol> <li><strong>Rehearse restoration</strong> in the VM using separate addresses and test data where appropriate.</li> <li><strong>Stop production writes</strong> during the agreed outage window and take the final consistent backup.</li> <li><strong>Restore and validate</strong> application data, permissions, credentials, and required hardware access.</li> <li><strong>Switch service routing</strong> after the replacement passes application-specific checks.</li> <li><strong>Keep the original stopped</strong> while retaining its configuration and recovery data.</li> <li><strong>Document rollback handling</strong> for data written after cutover before restarting the old system.</li> </ol> <p>Avoid <strong>two active writers</strong> against the same database storage. A rollback involving new production data requires a plan for preserving or intentionally discarding those writes. Merely restarting an old container does not reconcile two diverging data histories.</p> <h2 id="test-more-than-uptime"> <a href="#test-more-than-uptime" title="Test More Than Uptime">Test More Than Uptime</a> <a href="#test-more-than-uptime" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Test More Than Uptime">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Acceptance tests</strong> should follow the service’s purpose. A green container status establishes a running process. A usable service also requires its data, network access, dependencies, and recovery behavior.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Test</th> <th>Evidence to retain</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Application function</strong></td> <td>A successful real transaction, query, or media operation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Data completeness</strong></td> <td>Expected records, files, permissions, and recent changes</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Guest reboot</strong></td> <td>Services return without manual repair</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Backup restoration</strong></td> <td>The restored copy completes the same functional check</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Representative load</strong></td> <td>Latency, CPU, memory pressure, and storage behavior</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Maintenance rehearsal</strong></td> <td>A tested update and a usable recovery procedure</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Longer observation</strong></td> <td>Availability records spanning several previous failure intervals</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Worked decision:</strong> A camera service and an experimental downloader currently share one nested stack. Moving both into one VM improves kernel separation but preserves a shared guest-maintenance boundary. If camera availability is the priority, evaluate separate maintenance groups and resource limits, then test recording continuity during downloader updates.</p> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> The best placement follows the service dependency you need to isolate. Two VMs on one physical server still share its power, storage, and host kernel.
